Yes — your answer is correct.

In this section the bulky pink intimal plaque (the most advanced part of the atheroma) sits over a region where the underlying wall is visibly thinner. Beneath the heaviest plaque the medial layer — the contractile/elastic component (the smooth‑muscle and elastic "reserve" of the vessel wall, which is what is meant here by the energy/contractile stores) — is attenuated and atrophic, whereas in less affected areas the same layer is more intact.

Why this happens:
- The growing plaque narrows the lumen and compresses/obstructs the vasa vasorum, reducing the blood (and nutrient/oxygen) supply to the deeper wall.
- With poor perfusion and loss of trophic support, the smooth‑muscle cells and elastic fibers of the media underneath the worst plaque degenerate and the layer thins.
- Consequently the thinnest, most atrophic segment of the wall lies directly beneath the thickest, most advanced plaque — exactly what the image shows.

So the statement "the energy/contractile stores are thinned under the most advanced plaque" is **yes**.

(One terminology note: in standard histological language this layer is usually described as the *media* or the *elastic/muscular layer* rather than "energy stores"; the meaning in your question is the same.)
